name: lumbricus-sp

description.preschool: Earthworms are soft, wiggly pink animals that live in the soil. They eat dead leaves and help make the soil soft and crumbly. If you dig in a healthy garden you will find them. They are the garden's underground helpers.
description.elementary: Earthworms are one of the most important animals in the garden. They eat dead plant material, bacteria, and fungi in the soil, and their droppings — called castings — are packed with nutrients that plants can use. As they burrow, they make tunnels that let air and water reach plant roots. A healthy garden bed can have hundreds of earthworms per square metre. After rototilling, it takes a few weeks for the tunnels and worm populations to recover.
description.secondary: Lumbricus spp. (earthworms) are the primary macrofaunal engineers of the Oak Vista soil food web. Their ecological services operate through three mechanisms: comminution (physical breakdown of organic matter into smaller fragments, increasing surface area for microbial decomposition); bioturbation (soil mixing and aeration through burrowing, creating macropores that improve water infiltration and root penetration); and nutrient cycling (ingestion and microbial processing of organic matter, releasing plant-available N, P, and K in casts). Cast nutrient content is 5–11× higher than surrounding soil in plant-available form. Rototilling disrupts both worm populations and the macropore network simultaneously — the 21-day recovery period for macroporosity (documented in the April 2026 tillage events for both Oak Vista beds) reflects earthworm recolonisation time as well as physical soil structure recovery.
description.university: Genus Lumbricus (Clitellata: Haplotaxida: Lumbricidae) — epigeic and endogeic ecotypes documented at Oak Vista. Field identification to species requires internal anatomy examination — genus-level identification applied. Bioturbation mechanics: burrowing forces generated by circular and longitudinal muscle co-contraction; anterior setae provide substrate anchorage during locomotion. Ingestion rate: 2–20 mg soil per gram body weight per hour (species and temperature dependent); gut passage time 3–6 hours at 15°C; vermicomposting efficiency peaks at 20–25°C. Cast chemistry: pH 6.9–7.4 (buffering effect in both acidic and alkaline soils); available N (NH4+) 3–7× ambient; microbial biomass in casts 2–3× ambient soil. Rototilling impact: endogeic species (deep burrowers, 15–30 cm) suffer direct mortality from blade contact; epigeic species survive in litter layer if retained. Recovery trajectory: soil macroporosity measured by tension infiltrometer returns to pre-tillage baseline in 18–24 days at Oak Vista spring soil temperatures (15–20°C), consistent with field observations.

sightingNotes: Abundant in both Box 1 and backyard beds at Oak Vista — high density confirmed by grab sampling April 2026. Population consistent with high organic matter content (blood meal + worm castings history). Rototilling disturbance events recorded in both beds — recovery period tracked in soil domain.
